narrative:
The model predicted a 72% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year law school grades had the strongest influence. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class—far below the average of accepted students, who typically ranked around the middle of their class. This low academic standing strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.3 worked in the opposite direction. It sits slightly above the average of accepted students (3.23), so the model saw this as a modest positive signal that slightly increased the chance you might pass.

Your family’s upper-middle income bracket also provided a small positive nudge. While this is the most common income group among accepted students, its helpful effect was not large enough to offset the academic concerns.

In short, the model concluded that your law school performance so far indicates a high likelihood of struggling with the bar exam. To strengthen future applications, you should focus on improving your academic performance, seek additional bar preparation resources, or consider retaking key courses to raise your class ranking before reapplying.
